title: The history of the transistor, from 1947 to the first microprocessor
summary: A timeline-first walk from the 1947 point-contact transistor to the early microprocessors that put a CPU on one chip.

blocks.title: From a bench demo to a computer on a chip
blocks.body: The transistor did not leap from crystal radios to smartphones in one step. This page uses a timeline as the spine: 1947 at Bell Labs through the early 1970s microprocessors. The essays hang off the dates.

items.title: Point-contact transistor
items.detail: Bardeen and Brattain at Bell Labs demonstrate amplification in a germanium point-contact device; Shockley's role in the junction idea follows immediately in the lab's story.

items.title: Junction transistor theory → practice
items.detail: Shockley's junction transistor concepts move toward manufacturable bipolar devices that are more stable than point-contact oddities.

items.title: Silicon junction traction
items.detail: Silicon devices begin displacing germanium in many roles — higher temperature capability matters for real products.

items.title: Integrated circuit ideas
items.detail: Kilby (hybrid IC demonstration) and Noyce (planar IC approach at Fairchild) open the path from discrete transistors to many devices on one chip.

items.title: Planar process + Moore's observation
items.detail: Planar manufacturing scales complexity. Moore notes the economic pattern of rising component counts — denser chips become the industry's metronome.

items.title: Intel 4004
items.detail: A 4-bit CPU on a chip for calculators — often cited as the first commercial microprocessor.

items.title: 8-bit follow-ons
items.detail: 8008 and then 8080 (and contemporaries elsewhere) turn microprocessors into general-purpose building blocks, not only calculator brains.

blocks.heading: Why 1947 is the opening bell
blocks.body: Vacuum tubes already amplified. What the transistor offered was solid-state amplification without a glowing filament: smaller, cooler, eventually cheaper and more reliable at scale. The first devices were finicky. The historical break is still real — a solid crystal structure doing what hot glass envelopes had done.

blocks.caption: History has more contributors than any short table. This is a reader's map, not a patent docket.

columns.name: Germanium early devices
columns.detail: Worked, taught the industry, and struggled with temperature and leakage compared with what silicon would allow.

columns.name: Silicon ascent
columns.detail: Better high-temperature behavior and a manufacturing ecosystem that learned oxide, diffusion, and planar tricks.

columns.name: Why it matters on this timeline
columns.detail: Without manufacturable silicon processes, the IC and microprocessor chapters stay laboratory curiosities.

nodes.title: Discrete transistors
nodes.detail: One device per package; computers are rooms of them.

nodes.title: Integrated circuits
nodes.detail: Many devices share a die — logic building blocks shrink.

nodes.title: Microprocessor
nodes.detail: CPU datapath and control land on one chip — computers become boards, then boxes.

blocks.heading: What "first microprocessor" usually means here
blocks.body: The Intel 4004 (1971) is the conventional classroom landmark: a CPU designed as a general programmable chip for a calculator family, sold as a component. Contemporaneous and near-term chips complicate any absolute "first," which is why this timeline says "first microprocessor era" as much as a single trophy. The break with discrete TTL CPUs is what matters for the story.

items.label: Process idea that made density practical

blocks.quote: The timeline is the argument: amplification in a crystal, then many crystals on one die, then a computer's brain on one die.

blocks.heading: What changed for everyone else
blocks.body: Each jump on the timeline moved reliability and cost. Radios shrank. Computers left glass rooms. Controllers migrated into appliances. The reflective point is not nostalgia — it is that "smaller and cooler" compounded until software became the scarce resource instead of vacuum tubes.

blocks.heading: Timeline check
blocks.prompt: On this page's spine, what sits between discrete transistors and the microprocessor?
options: The integrated circuit / planar manufacturing era
blocks.explanation: ICs and planar processes made dense logic practical before a CPU could fit on one chip.
blocks.correctFeedback: Right — IC era is the bridge on the spine.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Look at the diagram Discrete → IC → microprocessor.

blocks.body: If you only remember the dates — 1947, planar ICs, 1971 — you can hang any deeper biography on the right peg.
